transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I’m here because my husband insisted, to be perfectly honest with you. He thinks I’m just getting worked up over nothing, but if you lived in my house, you’d see it too. It’s the kitchen. We started a remodel—oh, it has to be nearly two years ago now. Two whole years! You’d think a simple kitchen update would take a month, maybe two if there are delays, right? But no. 

And it’s not just incompetence, doctor, which is what my husband wants to believe. I’m absolutely sure of it now. The contractor we hired, he’s been quietly working together with some of the people right on our block. Our own neighbors! I've seen them talking. They’re all in on it to cheat us. They are deliberately keeping my kitchen half-wrong on purpose. Every time the crew comes over, something else is left unfinished or done backwards, like installing the cabinet doors so they hit the refrigerator, or leaving the trim off the baseboards. 

And they give me all these excuses—oh, the materials are backordered, or the measurements from the factory were wrong, just endless stories! It’s complete nonsense. My husband keeps pulling out his little file folder and showing me the receipts, pointing at the dates and the costs, trying to prove to me that it's just normal business and we haven't paid for the unfinished parts yet. But a receipt doesn't explain what's really going on. They want to keep my house in a state of ruin to bleed us dry and make a fool of me, and no matter how many excuses they give or papers my husband waves in my face, I know exactly what they are doing.
Do you think anyone else believes that your neighbors and the contractor are working together against you?

Well, no... no, I don't suppose they do. And that’s really the most frustrating part of this whole ordeal, doctor. You try to explain it to people, you lay it all out for them perfectly logically, and they just look at you with these blank stares. 

I was talking to my sister, Linda—she lives over in Ohio, we talk on the phone every Sunday afternoon, usually right after I get back from church—and I was telling her about the latest incident with the plumbing under the sink. I explained how the crew left the pipes completely unsealed so water would slowly drip and ruin the new flooring we just put down. And Linda, bless her heart, she just sighed and said, "Oh, maybe they just forgot the plumber's putty." Forgot the putty! As if a licensed professional just forgets how to do the most basic part of his job. 

So no, I haven't found anyone else who sees the truth of it. My husband certainly doesn't, as I told you. He’s a good man, but he just wants to keep the peace. He’s always been like that, never wanting to make a fuss or rock the boat with the neighbors. And the other folks on the street who aren't involved... well, they're just too wrapped up in their own little lives, mowing their lawns and walking their dogs, to notice what's happening right under their noses. It makes you feel so terribly alone, you know? When you can see something so clearly, as plain as day, and everyone around you is just walking around with blinders on. I just... I don't even know who else I could try to talk to about it anymore without them treating me like I'm just some complaining old woman who doesn't understand construction.
Do you think it's possible that the contractor and your neighbors might not be working together against you?

Well... I mean, people always ask that, don't they? "Are you sure? Could it just be a mistake?" But no. No, doctor, I really don't think it's possible that I'm wrong about this. I mean, you just have to look at the sheer timeline and the scale of it all. 

For nearly two years now—ever since the fall of the year before last, right around the time the maple tree in our front yard started dropping its leaves—I’ve been completely, one-hundred-percent sure of what's going on. You don't just have two whole years of "accidents." The contractor and some of those people on my block, especially the ones two doors down who always have those loud barbecues on the weekends, they have been quietly working together this entire time just to cheat us. It's so obvious when you actually pay attention to the details. They are purposely, deliberately keeping my kitchen half-wrong. On purpose! 

Just last week, for example, they finally came to put in the new light fixtures we ordered months ago, but they wired them so the switch by the hallway door turns on the little pendant light over the sink instead of the main overhead lights. Who does that? A professional doesn't do that by accident. 

And my husband... oh, my poor husband, he means well, he really does, but he'll sit there at the kitchen island—the half-finished island, I should say, because it's still missing the end panels—and he'll pull out his little calculator and his manila folder of paperwork. But no matter how many receipts my husband shows me, pointing at the numbers and the paid invoices, or how many ridiculous excuses they give us about shipping delays from the warehouse or factory errors... it doesn't change what I know in my bones. You can forge a receipt, you can make up a story about a truck breaking down, but you can't explain away the sheer malice of it all. They are doing this to me intentionally. So, no, doctor. I don't think it's just a misunderstanding or bad luck. I know exactly what they're up to, even if nobody else wants to open their eyes and see it.
Have you ever thought that there might be something wrong with your own thinking or perception about the situation with your kitchen remodel?

Well, no... no, I haven't. Why would I? I mean, I know my husband thinks I’m just getting myself all worked up, and my sister Linda thinks I’m making mountains out of molehills, but... but there's nothing wrong with my thinking. My mind is perfectly fine, doctor. I’m 67 years old, I’ve raised three children, I managed a household for forty years—I think I know when someone is trying to pull the wool over my eyes! 

I mean, if you were in my shoes, and you saw the same contractor pulling into the driveway of the house two doors down—the ones with the loud barbecues, like I mentioned—and standing there in the driveway, talking and pointing at my house... well, what else are you supposed to think? It's not a problem with my perception. My eyes work just fine, thank you very much. I had my vision checked just last spring at the optometrist over in the strip mall by the grocery store, and Dr. Higgins said my prescription hasn't even changed. 

So no, I don't think there's anything wrong with my mind. It’s just... it’s incredibly frustrating when you’re the only one who can see the forest for the trees. You try to show people the evidence—the backwards doors, the unsealed pipes, the completely nonsensical wiring—and they just want to write it off as incompetence or bad luck. But I know what I see. I know what's happening in my own home. And it just breaks my heart that my own husband would rather believe a pile of paper receipts than his own wife's two eyes. So, no, doctor. My thinking is perfectly clear. It's everyone else who seems to be living in a fantasy world where contractors just accidentally ruin a kitchen for two solid years.
Have you ever felt like someone was out to get you or plotting against you in a situation outside of the kitchen remodel?

Oh, goodness, no. No, nothing like that. Why would anyone be out to get me in general? I'm just an ordinary woman, doctor. I go to church on Sundays, I keep a neat house, I talk to my sister Linda on the phone... I mean, before all this nonsense with the kitchen started, my life was perfectly quiet. Peaceful, even. 

I've never had trouble with people plotting against me before. I mean, sure, you have little disagreements here and there—like the time a few years back when the woman who runs the bake sale for the church bazaar, Mrs. Gable, she tried to tell me my pecan pie wasn't "traditional" enough because I use a splash of bourbon in the filling. Can you imagine? I’ve been making that pie since 1982, and suddenly it's not traditional! But that was just petty jealousy, not a plot. She just wanted her own daughter's cherry pie to be the centerpiece of the dessert table. I saw right through that, but it wasn't a conspiracy. Just small-town church politics, you know how that goes. 

But no, nobody has ever tried to ruin my life or trick me like this contractor and those neighbors are doing. That's why it's so shocking! That's why I can't just let it go, no matter how much my husband begs me to just "trust the process." Trust the process? When they're clearly doing it on purpose? 

Before this remodel, I trusted people. I really did. I thought if you paid a professional good money—and let me tell you, we paid a small fortune for those custom cabinets, the ones with the soft-close hinges that they still haven't aligned properly—I thought they would do the job right. I never would have imagined that a group of people could be so spiteful, so dedicated to making one woman's life miserable, just over a kitchen. So, no, doctor. I've never felt this way about anything else, because nothing like this has ever happened to me before. It's just this kitchen. Just this one, unending nightmare of a kitchen remodel.
Have you ever had thoughts that people were plotting against you outside of the situation with your kitchen?

Like I was just saying, doctor, absolutely not. I know we just touched on this, but really, outside of dealing with the remodel, I still keep up with my church gatherings, my book club, my regular household routines, and my family plans exactly the way I usually do. I mean, my goodness, just because I have a contractor trying to ruin my kitchen doesn't mean I stop living my life! 

I still go to Sunday service every single week, and I still go to my Wednesday morning women's group. And my book club—we meet on the second Thursday of every month at the community center, and right now we are reading this very thick historical biography. Margaret always dominates the conversation and talks entirely too much about her own cats, bless her heart, but nobody there is plotting against me. We just drink our tea and talk about the chapters. 

And as for my household routines, well, I am very particular about keeping a tidy home, and that hasn't changed one bit. I still vacuum the living room and the guest bedrooms on Tuesdays, and I dust the dining room on Thursdays, even if the kitchen is blocked off with that awful plastic sheeting and covered in drywall dust. I haven't let my standards slip at all. 

And I still make all our family plans, too. I organize the Sunday dinners, even if we have to order a pizza and eat takeout in the living room because my stove is disconnected and the dining area is full of uninstalled cabinet doors. I still coordinate all the visits with my grandchildren, and I still call my sister Linda every Sunday evening. 

Everything else in my life is completely, perfectly normal. It's really just this one specific situation with the kitchen and those neighbors. So no, I don't walk around thinking the mailman or the ladies at the church are out to get me. I'm a very grounded person, doctor, I really am. It's just that when someone is blatantly tampering with your home right in front of your face, you have to speak up about it.
Have you ever had thoughts that people were plotting against you in situations unrelated to your kitchen remodel or your neighbors?

Doctor, I feel like we are going around in circles here. I really do. I mean, I just answered this, didn't I? I feel like I'm repeating myself, but maybe I didn't explain it clearly enough the first time. No. The answer is no. I have never, not once, felt like anyone was plotting against me in any other part of my life. 

I mean, honestly, who has the time for that? And who would want to? Like I said, I’m just a retired woman trying to live her life. I don’t have enemies at the grocery store, the mailman isn't tampering with my letters—he’s a lovely young man named Kevin who always waves when he drops off the catalogs—and the people at my church are just regular, everyday people. I mean, sure, sometimes Mrs. Higgins at the front pew sings a little too loud and off-key during the hymns, and it can be a bit grating, especially when we’re doing "How Great Thou Art," but she’s not doing it to torture me. She just has a loud voice. 

There are no grand conspiracies in my life, doctor. None. It is literally just this one, specific, horrible situation with the contractor and those neighbors two doors down. That’s it. If they would just finish the kitchen—if they would just put the pipes where they belong and stop installing the cabinet doors backwards on purpose to mock me—I wouldn't be here talking to you at all. I’d be at home, baking a pie in my new oven, living my completely normal, perfectly quiet life. So, I don't know how else to say it... no. Nobody else is plotting against me. It's just the kitchen. Just the kitchen.
Have you ever held a belief that you knew to be true, but others did not, outside of the situation with your kitchen remodel?

I... well, no, doctor. Not at all. I mean, what kind of belief are you talking about? Like a secret? Because I don't have any grand secrets about the world, if that's what you're getting at. I'm not one of those people who thinks they know something everyone else doesn't, like those folks you see on the television talking about aliens or government cover-ups or what have you. Goodness, no. 

I'm a very practical woman. If it's raining outside, I believe it's raining, and so does my husband, and so does everyone else with eyes. I don't go around inventing things. I mean, I suppose there was the time I was absolutely certain that the local bakery changed the recipe for their sourdough bread—they used to have this wonderful, thick crust, and then suddenly it was soft, almost like sandwich bread. I brought it up to the girl behind the counter, and she swore up and down they hadn't changed a thing. My husband thought I was just being picky, but I *knew* the texture was different. I brought it up at book club, and Margaret—you remember I mentioned Margaret, the one with the cats—she said it tasted exactly the same to her. But that's just a matter of having a refined palate, isn't it? That's not some... some bizarre conviction. I just know my bread, doctor. I've been baking since I was a teenager, so of course I'd notice a change in the yeast or the proofing time before someone like Margaret would. 

But aside from little everyday things like that—just having a stronger opinion or a better eye for detail than other people—no, I don't hold any strange beliefs that nobody else shares. I see the world exactly the way it is. Which is why it is so endlessly frustrating that nobody else seems to see what is happening right in front of them with this remodel! It's clear as day! But outside of that? No. Just the kitchen. Everything else in my life is completely ordinary and I agree with everyone else just fine.
Have you ever had a period of time where you held a fixed belief that was not based in reality, outside of the situation with your kitchen remodel?

Doctor, I really feel like you're trying to catch me in some kind of trap here. A fixed belief not based in reality? No, of course not! I just told you, I'm a very practical, grounded person. I don't go around imagining things or making up fairy tales. 

I mean, I've lived a very long, very ordinary life up until this whole nightmare started. I raised three children, I kept a beautiful home, I volunteered at the church bake sales for thirty-five years—I was the one who organized the schedule for the pie booths, mind you, because nobody else could keep track of who was bringing cherry and who was bringing apple, and you can't have five cherry pies and no apple, that's just poor planning. But that's just being organized, that's not... a fixed belief not based in reality. 

Everything I believe, everything I know, is based on exactly what I see and hear. If I see the contractor whispering to my neighbor over the fence, and then the next day my new sink is suddenly scratched, well, that's reality, isn't it? That's putting two and two together. But outside of that? No. I don't think the sky is green, I don't think my husband is a secret agent, I don't think the television is talking to me. I just want my kitchen finished properly so I can go back to my normal life. I really don't know why we keep going over this, doctor. I am completely fine, except for the fact that my home is being sabotaged.
Have you ever had any other beliefs that you were completely certain of, but turned out to be incorrect?

Incorrect? I... well, no. I really don't think so. I mean, goodness, everyone makes little mistakes, don't they? If you mean little things, sure. Like... oh, just last month, I was absolutely positive I had bought a spare bottle of Dawn dish soap—the blue kind, mind you, I only use the blue kind because the green one smells too much like artificial apples and it gives my husband a terrible headache—and I was so sure I put it under the laundry room sink. I looked everywhere. I could have sworn on a stack of Bibles it was there. But it turned out I had left it in the trunk of the Buick and it had rolled all the way back under the spare tire compartment. 

So, I suppose I was incorrect about *that*. But that’s just... that's just being forgetful for a moment, isn't it? A slip of the mind. That’s not a *belief*. 

When it comes to things that actually matter, things I am completely certain of... no, I don't go around being wrong about those. I'm a very careful person, doctor. I don't jump to conclusions. I observe, I take notes, I pay attention to the details. That’s exactly why this whole situation with the kitchen is so incredibly upsetting! Because I *know* what I'm seeing. If I were the kind of flighty woman who just imagined things and was constantly being proven wrong, well, maybe I wouldn't trust my own eyes. But I have a lifetime of being sensible and correct behind me. My husband always says, "If you want the straight facts, ask Helen," and he's right. 

So, no. I don't have these incorrect beliefs you keep searching for. I haven't been wrong about anything important, and I am certainly not wrong about what those contractors are doing to my home. I really think we are just beating a dead horse with these questions, I honestly do.
Have you ever had any other experiences where you felt like something strange or unusual was happening to you, but others didn't seem to notice or understand?

Strange or unusual? Like... like what, exactly? I mean, life is full of little oddities, isn't it? But if you mean something bizarre happening *to* me, personally, while everyone else is just oblivious... no. No, I really haven't. 

I mean, I suppose there was the time, oh, maybe fifteen years ago, when I was absolutely convinced the dry cleaner on 4th Street—the one that used to be next to the old Woolworths before they tore it down to build that dreadful modern bank—I was convinced they were using a different starch on my husband's collars. He likes a very stiff collar, you see, he always has. And for three weeks in a row, they came back just a little bit limp. Not terrible, but not right. I pointed it out to him, and he just shrugged and said they seemed fine to him. I even brought it up to the owner, Mr. Higgins, a lovely man, God rest his soul, but he swore they hadn't changed suppliers. I felt like I was the only one in the world who could feel the difference in the cotton! But that wasn't something *strange* happening to me, that was just... well, that was just me paying attention to the laundry. 

I don't have things happen to me that are... what did you say? Unusual? No. I don't have ghosts moving my furniture, I don't have strange men following me at the grocery store, I don't have mysterious illnesses that the doctors can't explain. My life has been wonderfully, blessedly boring, doctor. Right up until we decided to update the kitchen. And even then, what's happening isn't "strange" in some spooky, mysterious way. It's very straightforward sabotage. It's malicious, yes, and it's infuriating, but it's not some... some bizarre phenomenon that I'm just imagining while everyone else goes about their day. It's happening right there in my house, with real tools and real people, even if my husband refuses to see it. But before this? No. Nothing strange at all. Just a very normal life.
Have you ever held any other beliefs that you were completely certain of, but were later proven to be false?

Doctor, I feel like we are going around in circles here. Are you asking me the same question just to see if I change my answer? Because I won't. I don't change my story because my story is the truth. 

I don't have beliefs that are proven false. I just don't. I mean, think about it logically—if I were the sort of person who was constantly absolutely certain of things that turned out to be completely wrong, how would I have managed to run a household for forty-five years? How would I have managed the finances, making sure every penny was accounted for and we never overdrew the checking account, not even once, not even when the transmission went out on the station wagon back in '88 and we had to scramble to find a mechanic who wouldn't overcharge us? You don't get through life successfully by believing things that aren't true.

I am a very sensible woman. My mother was a sensible woman, my grandmother was a sensible woman. We don't do... flights of fancy. If I believe something, it's because I have seen the evidence with my own two eyes. Just like I saw the sawdust swept under the new refrigerator, which the contractor swore he cleaned up, but I found it, didn't I? Because I know what I'm looking for. 

So no, I haven't had any beliefs that were proven false. I really think we should be talking about how to stop those men from ruining my cabinets, instead of digging through my past trying to find a time I was wrong about something. Because you're not going to find it, doctor. You're just not.
Have you ever been diagnosed with or treated for any mental health conditions in the past?

Mental health conditions? Oh, goodness, no. Heavens, no. I mean, why on earth would I have been? I've just spent the last ten minutes explaining to you how incredibly sensible and grounded I am, haven't I? 

I have never—not once in my entire sixty-seven years on this earth—needed to see a psychiatrist or a therapist or a counselor or whatever it is people are calling themselves these days. My generation, doctor, we didn't go running to a professional every time we felt a little sad or overwhelmed. If you had a problem, you dealt with it. You talked to your husband, or you talked to your sister—my sister Margaret, God rest her soul, was a wonderful listener, she could always talk sense into me if I was getting worked up over nothing, like the time the church ladies auxiliary tried to change the date of the annual bake sale without consulting the committee. But that's just normal life stress! That's not a *condition*. 

I've never been diagnosed with anything like that because there's nothing to diagnose. My mind is perfectly sound. I don't have depression, I don't have anxiety... well, I suppose I have a bit of anxiety *now*, but who wouldn't, with strangers coming into their home and deliberately destroying perfectly good oak cabinetry? But that's a normal reaction to a terrible situation, not a mental illness. 

I take my blood pressure medication—lisinopril, ten milligrams, every morning with a piece of toast—and I take a multivitamin, and that is it. I don't take pills for my mood, I don't go to therapy, and I certainly don't have any mental health conditions. I'm just a normal woman trying to protect her home, doctor. That's all this is.
Have you ever had any other experiences where you believed something was happening to you that others did not believe?

Doctor, we really are just beating a dead horse here, aren't we? It feels like you keep asking me the exact same question, just dressing it up in different words. "Something strange happening," "beliefs proven false," "things others didn't believe"... it's all the same thing, isn't it? And my answer is still the same. No. 

I don't go around imagining things. I don't live in a fantasy world where I think the postman is a spy or the television is talking to me. I've told you, I am a very practical person. When we bought our house in 1978—it was a lovely little ranch, still is, really, just needed a bit of updating, which is how this whole nightmare started—but when we bought it, the inspector said the roof had another ten years on it. I went up into the attic myself, with a flashlight, and I saw the water stains on the rafters. I told my husband, I told the realtor, and they both said, "Oh, it's just old stains, the roof is fine." They didn't believe me! They thought I was just being a fussy woman. But I insisted we get a roofer out there, and what do you know? The flashing around the chimney was completely rusted through. If we had waited, the first big storm would have ruined the plaster in the living room. 

So yes, there have been times when people didn't believe me at first. But that's not because I was imagining things, it's because men—and it's usually men, doctor, let's be honest—don't like to listen to a woman who knows what she's talking about. But I was proven right. Just like I'm going to be proven right about these contractors. 

My husband, bless him, he just wants the kitchen finished so he can have his morning coffee in peace. He doesn't want to see the little scratches they're leaving on the inside of the drawers, or the way the hinges on the pantry door are just slightly misaligned so they'll wear out faster. He thinks I'm being too demanding. He doesn't believe they're doing it on purpose to get back at me for making them redo the tile grout. But he'll see. Eventually, when the doors start falling off, he'll see I was right all along. 

But as for some... some grand delusion that nobody else believes? No. Absolutely not. I only believe what is right in front of my face. And I really think you should start believing me too, doctor, because I am not crazy, I am just very, very observant.
Have you ever had a belief about something unrelated to your kitchen remodel that you were completely certain of, but others did not believe?

Unrelated to the kitchen? Well, no, of course not. Because like I keep trying to tell you, I don't just go around making things up or having wild ideas about every little thing in the world. I am not that kind of person, doctor. I'm just dealing with a very specific, very real situation right in my own home, and I am not going to just let it go. 

In fact, the only reason I’m even here in this office today is because for nearly two years now... yes, almost two full years of living in an absolute nightmare of a construction zone... I’ve been absolutely sure that the contractor and some of the people on my block have been quietly working together to cheat us. I know it sounds terrible to say, but I have been watching them. I see my neighbor Susan whispering with the foreman by the property line, and then the very next day, suddenly the wrong drawer pulls are installed again or the measurements are off by half an inch. 

They are deliberately keeping my kitchen half-wrong on purpose. It is a coordinated effort to drag this project out, drain our savings, and just drive me to my wit's end. 

And my husband, bless his heart, he just wants peace and quiet, so he refuses to see what is happening right under his nose. He pulls out his manila folder and points to all the paperwork, showing me receipt after receipt, trying to explain the math to me like I'm a child. But no matter how many receipts my husband shows me, or how many flimsy excuses they give him about supply chain delays or backordered materials or misunderstood blueprints, I know exactly what is going on. They are working together to cheat us, and he is just letting them do it. 

So no, doctor, I don't have beliefs about other unrelated things. I just have the truth about my kitchen, and it is frankly exhausting trying to get anyone to simply open their eyes and see what is happening right in front of them.
Have you ever had a belief that you held to be true, but was later proven to be false?

Proven to be false? Doctor, I really must ask, are you actually listening to a word I am saying, or are you just reading off a list of questions on your clipboard? Because I feel like we are just going in circles now. 

I don't hold "false" beliefs. I don't just invent fairy tales in my head. Like I literally just finished telling you not two minutes ago, the entire reason I am sitting in this office today is because for nearly two years now, I’ve been absolutely sure that the contractor and some of the people on my block have been quietly working together to cheat us. And they are doing it to keep my kitchen half-wrong on purpose. That is a fact. It is happening right in my own home.

Now, my husband—bless his heart, he tries—he thinks he can prove me false. He really does. He sits down at the dining room table... well, we have to use the dining room table for everything now because the kitchen is an absolute disaster zone... and he pulls out that thick manila folder of his. He thinks he's proving me wrong with his little calculator! But I tell you, no matter how many receipts my husband shows me, or how many ridiculous excuses they give him about backorders or shipping delays or whatever nonsense they've made up this week, it doesn't change what I can see with my own two eyes. 

A piece of paper from a hardware store with some numbers on it doesn't prove me false, doctor. It just proves they are very good at covering their tracks and making everything look official. He thinks a receipt means they aren't cheating us, but that's just because he doesn't want to deal with the conflict. So, no. I haven't had a belief proven false. I am just the only one willing to look past the excuses and see the truth of what they're doing to us.
Have you ever had a belief that something was happening to you or someone you know that others did not believe, outside of the situation with your kitchen remodel?

Doctor, for heaven's sake! Are you... are you feeling quite alright yourself? Because you literally just asked me that exact same question not five minutes ago! "Unrelated to the kitchen," "outside of the situation with the kitchen"... it is the exact same question, just rearranged! 

I really feel like I am talking to a brick wall here. I mean, are you writing any of this down on that notepad of yours, or are you just waiting for your turn to speak? Because I have been very, very clear with you. I am not some hysterical woman who goes around making up stories about her neighbors or thinking the sky is falling. I had a perfectly normal, quiet life before all of this started. I enjoyed my garden, I kept a nice home, I minded my own business. 

So, for the absolute last time, no. There is nothing else. The only reason I am here—the only reason my husband made such a fuss and insisted I come talk to you—is because for nearly two years now, I’ve been sure the contractor and some people on my block have been quietly working together to cheat us. That is the one and only issue. They are coordinating this whole thing to keep my kitchen half-wrong on purpose. 

And it doesn't matter what anyone else thinks. It doesn't matter no matter how many receipts my husband shows me from that overstuffed folder of his, or how many excuses they give him about why the crown molding doesn't match or why the plumbing had to be ripped out a third time. I see what they are doing. 

I really don't know how else to explain it to you, doctor. There are no other situations. There are no other secret beliefs. There is just my kitchen, those contractors, and the people on my street who are trying to ruin me. Now, can we please move on from this question, because my throat is getting dry from repeating myself.
Have you ever had a belief that something was real or true, but later found out it was not, before this situation with your kitchen remodel?

Doctor, I... I honestly don't know what to say to you anymore. I feel like I'm trapped in some sort of loop. Did you not hear me just now? Or the time before that? You are asking me the exact same thing again! "Before this situation," "outside of this situation," "proven false"... it's all the same question! 

I am a sixty-seven-year-old woman. I have lived a very long, very ordinary life. I raised my children, I kept a lovely home, I volunteered at the church bake sales. I didn't go around having... having strange beliefs or making up stories about things being real when they weren't. I just lived my life. A normal, quiet life. 

There is nothing before the kitchen. There is nothing outside the kitchen. There is no history of me being some sort of... of crazy person who imagines things! The only reason we are even having this conversation—the only reason I am sitting in this uncomfortable chair in this office—is because of what is happening right now, in my house, with those contractors and my neighbors. 

I just... I don't understand why you keep trying to dig up something from my past that simply isn't there. Are you trying to prove that I have a habit of making things up? Because I don't. I never have. I am just a woman trying to get her kitchen finished after two years of being cheated and lied to, and nobody will listen to me. Not my husband, and clearly, not you either.
